units.translation: In the datives ἡμῖν [to us] (and likewise ὑμῖν [to you]) the second syllable is sometimes shortened for the sake of the meter, with the accent changed to ἡμίν and ὑμίν: a license which Aeschylus in the surviving plays used once (Eum. 347 ἁμὶν ἐκράνθη [it was accomplished for us] in a dactylic verse), Euripides never, but Sophocles in many places: on which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 135a. Aeschylus also once used the Doric ἄμμι [to us] in a dochmiac verse, Sept. 156 τί πόλις τις ἄμμι πάσχει; [what does the city suffer for us?], where most copies have ἄμμιν.
on which see Apollonius on pronouns p. 61 and Etym. M. p. 314, 52.
There is one example of the accusative ἐμέ γε [me at least]

The suspect form ἐγών [I], which the tragedians never used, is read in M Pers. 931 ὅδ᾽ ἐγὼν, οἰοῖ, αἰακτός [this I, alas, lamentable], where I restored ἐγώ with a hiatus before the interjection no less excusable than between οἰοî [alas] and αἰακτός [lamentable]. More absurdly at Suppl. 740 at the end of a trimeter σάφ ' οἶδ᾽ ἐγὼν [I know clearly] is written in M, where Turnebus restored ἐγώ.
For you the command of Zeus has its fulfillment indeed –, but I am without daring, etc.
And never cowering before harsh threats will I reveal this.
There I, planning the best course, to persuade
For I would not have wished to see these things –.
And indeed I am pitiful for my friends to look upon.
But in addition to these things I gave them fire.
Anticleia – I mean your mother, who bore you
Truly he will still have need of me —.
Such things when I spoke in my words.
And it struck my stern-faced modesty.
For you could learn everything from me.
Do not care for me more than what is sweet to me.
O ruler of many, son of Atreus, learn from me
No one of the gods is angry on my behalf,
For they are suppliants to my friends, not to me,
For you it is fated to be married, and for me to marry.
These things are not loathsome to me.
Who once hurled a missile at me –.
A heavenly scent, apart from perfumed vessels, breathing upon me.
For I know that those dearest to us two are bitter,
and the diseases of us two.
what does the city suffer for us?
I indeed will enrich this land.
And I myself will dance the prelude.
And I bid you fear my oracles.
And I your perfumes and unguents.
Not using me as a teacher, at least.
For me at least the springs of tears have been quenched.
He will not put me to death, at any rate.
on the one hand – on the other
and I, and of me, and me
